$x^4-2x^2+9$ & $V_4$ & $2-\tfrac{3L_3}{4}\approx 0.81128$ & $2-\tfrac{3L_3}{4}\approx 0.81128$ & $2$ & $\tfrac{3L_3}{4}$ \\
$\Phi_5$ & $C_4$ & $\tfrac32$ & $\tfrac32$ & $2$ & $\tfrac12$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketches]
\textbf{$S_3$.} The type census is $1,3,2$ out of $6$, giving $H(T) = \tfrac23+\tfrac{L_3}{2}$. The sign is a function of the type ($[1,1,1]$, $[3]$ even; $[2,1]$ odd), so Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} and Lemma~\ref{lem:lagrange} give $I = H(c) = 1$.

\textbf{$S_4$.} The census is $1,6,3,8,6$ for $[1,1,1,1],[2,1,1],[2,2],[3,1],[4]$ out of $24$, giving $H(T) = \tfrac32+\tfrac{3L_3}{8}$. Again the sign is a function of the type, so $I = 1$ exactly. Since the coset $A_4$ carries three types, Proposition~\ref{prop:deficit} gives $I < H(T)$ strictly.

\textbf{$A_4$.} The census is $1,3,8$ for $[1,1,1,1],[2,2],[3,1]$ out of $12$, giving $H(T)=\tfrac{3L_3}{4}$; the coset readout is balanced over three cosets, so $H(c) = L_3$; the identity and the three double transpositions form the trivial coset while the eight $3$-cycles split four-four between the two nontrivial cosets, giving $H(c,T) = \tfrac23 + \tfrac{3L_3}{4}$ and hence $I = L_3-\tfrac23$, loss $\tfrac23$. Structurally, the type $[3,1]$ fills both nontrivial cosets, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} the channel cannot be complete.

\textbf{$D_4$.} The census is $1$ identity, $2$ diagonal reflections of type $[2,1,1]$, $3$ elements of type $[2,2]$, $2$ four-cycles, giving $H(T) = \tfrac52-\tfrac{3L_3}{8}$; $H(c) = 2$ and $H(c,T)=\tfrac94$, whence $I = \tfrac94-\tfrac{3L_3}{8}$. The deficit comes from the three $[2,2]$ elements lying in different cosets.

\textbf{$V_4$, $C_4$.} Abelian, so $I = H(T)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:abelian}; the censuses $1,3$ and $1,1,2$ out of $4$ give $H(T) = 2-\tfrac{3L_3}{4}$ and $H(T) = \tfrac32$ respectively, with caps $2$ and losses $\tfrac{3L_3}{4}$, $\tfrac12$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The $S_4$ cap is about the abelianization]
The field $x^4-x-1$ satisfies $I(c;T) = 1 < \tfrac32+\tfrac38 L_3 = H(T)$: a five-type field with more than two bits of splitting entropy leaks exactly the one bit of its quadratic abelianization.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[The reversal]\label{cor:reversal}
$I_{V_4} = 2-\tfrac34 L_3 < \tfrac94-\tfrac38 L_3 = I_{D_4}$, and both are strictly below $2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The inequality reduces to $\tfrac38 L_3 > -\tfrac14$; the upper bounds reduce to $L_3 > 1$ and $L_3 > \tfrac23$.
\end{proof}

Corollary~\ref{cor:reversal} refutes the natural expectation that abelian fields carry richer channels. Under a structural ordering by branching of the factorization behaviour the pair $(V_4,D_4)$ is ordered $V_4 > D_4$; the type channels order it the other way. Both orderings are instances of the same law: the fields differ not in the availability of reciprocity but in how well their type readouts separate cosets.

\section{The semiprime level}

\subsection{The model}

A reader presented with a semiprime $N = pq$ sees the residue of $N$, which by multiplicativity of the abelian characters corresponds to the \emph{product} of the two Frobenius cosets, and the \emph{unordered} pair of splitting types $\{T(p),T(q)\}$ --- unordered, because such a reader has no canonical way to attribute a shape to a factor. Modelling the two Frobenius elements as an independent uniform pair $(x,y)\in G\times G$, the semiprime channel is
\[
I_2 := I\big(c(xy);\,\{T(x),T(y)\}\big),
\]
with ordered variant $I_2^{\mathrm{ord}} := I\big(c(xy);\,(T(x),T(y))\big)$.

\begin{theorem}[Semiprime closed forms]\label{thm:semi}
With $L_3=\log_2 3$ and $L_5 = \log_2 5$:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Field & $G$ & $I_2$ & numerically \\
\midrule
$x^3\pm x+1$ & $S_3$ & $1$ & $1.00000$ \\
$x^4-x-1$ & $S_4$ & $1$ & $1.00000$ \\
$x^4+8x+12$ & $A_4$ & $L_3-\tfrac{10}{9}$ & $0.47385$ \\
$x^4-2$ & $D_4$ & $\tfrac{39}{16}-\tfrac34 L_3 + \tfrac{5}{64}L_5$ & $1.43018$ \\
$x^4-2x^2+9$ & $V_4$ & $\tfrac{19}{8}-\tfrac{21}{16}L_3$ & $0.29474$ \\
$\Phi_5$ & $C_4$ & $\tfrac54$ & $1.25000$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
In each case the three entropies $H(c(xy))$, $H(\{T(x),T(y)\})$ and the joint entropy are evaluated by census over $G\times G$ (of sizes $36,576,144,64,16,16$). The coset readout of the product is balanced, since $xy$ is uniform on $G$ when $x$ is uniform, so $H(c(xy)) = \log_2[G:G']$ in every row. For $C_4$, for instance, the symmetric type census gives $H = \tfrac{19}{8}$, the joint entropy is $\tfrac{25}{8}$, and $I_2 = 2+\tfrac{19}{8}-\tfrac{25}{8} = \tfrac54$. The $D_4$ row is the only one producing a $\log_2 5$, from a cell of relative weight $5/64$ in the symmetric table.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The $C_2$ cap at the semiprime level]
The $S_3$ and $S_4$ fields deliver exactly one bit through a semiprime: a five-type $S_4$ field cannot beat a quadratic one, because the cap is a theorem about the abelianization.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Semiprime reversal]
$I_2(V_4) < I_2(D_4)$ and $I_2(S_4) < I_2(D_4)$: a non-abelian field exceeds one bit and outperforms both the abelian $V_4$ field and every field with quadratic abelianization.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Substituting the closed forms, the claims reduce to $1 < L_3 < 2 < L_5$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The which-factor wall]\label{thm:wall}
For each of the six fields,
\[ I\big(c(xy);\,(T(x),T(y))\big) = I\big(c(xy);\,\{T(x),T(y)\}\big). \]
Learning which prime factor carried which splitting shape is worth exactly zero bits.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both sides are evaluated by census; for each field the ordered and unordered type entropies differ by exactly the amount by which the corresponding joint entropies differ, so the difference cancels in $I = H(c)+H(\text{type})-H(\text{joint})$. For $C_4$: $H(\mathrm{ord}) = 3$, $H(c,\mathrm{ord}) = \tfrac{15}{4}$, so $I^{\mathrm{ord}} = 2+3-\tfrac{15}{4} = \tfrac54 = I_2$. Structurally, the coset of the product is a symmetric function of $(x,y)$, so the antisymmetric part of the ordered readout is independent of the residue given the multiset.
\end{proof}

\section{Numerical verification}

The closed forms are exact statements about uniform measures on finite groups; their arithmetic relevance rests on Chebotarev equidistribution, an asymptotic statement, so it is worth checking against honest primes.

\paragraph{Prime level.} The splitting type of each unramified prime below a bound is computed by distinct-degree factorization over $\mathbb{F}_p$: iteratively forming $\gcd(x^{p^{d}}-x, f_{\mathrm{rem}})$ for $d=1,2,\ldots$ extracts the product of the degree-$d$ irreducible factors. The residue dial is read from the maximal abelian subextension: the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{\disc}{p}\right)$ for the $S_3$ and $S_4$ fields, $p \bmod 8$ for $x^4-2$ (maximal abelian subextension $\mathbb{Q}(i,\sqrt2)$, conductor $8$), and $p \bmod 5$ for $\Phi_5$. Over the $6054$ primes below $6\cdot10^{4}$:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Field & $G$ & $H(T)$ measured & $I$ measured & law & difference \\
\midrule
$x^3+x+1$ & $S_3$ & $1.45608$ & $1.00000$ & $1.00000$ & $0.00000$ \\
$x^3-x+1$ & $S_3$ & $1.45619$ & $0.99998$ & $1.00000$ & $0.00002$ \\
$x^4-x-1$ & $S_4$ & $2.09112$ & $0.99985$ & $1.00000$ & $0.00015$ \\
$x^4-2$ & $D_4$ & $1.90554$ & $1.65930$ & $1.65564$ & $0.00366$ \\
$\Phi_5$ & $C_4$ & $1.49834$ & $1.49834$ & $1.50000$ & $0.00166$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Agreement is at the level of a few thousandths of a bit, consistent with the $O(1/n)$ upward bias of the plug-in estimator. An independent measurement over roughly $2.3\times10^{4}$ primes per field reproduced the seven prime-level values (counting both $S_3$ fields) as $1.0000$, $1.0000$, $1.0100$, $0.9188$, $1.6555$, $0.8092$, $1.4989$ against the laws $1$, $1$, $1$, $0.91830$, $1.65564$, $0.81128$, $1.5$.

\paragraph{Semiprime level.} Monte Carlo with $4\times10^{5}$ draws per field from unramified pools gives $1.0001$ (both $S_3$ fields), $1.0034$ ($S_4$), $0.4729$ ($A_4$), $1.4325$ ($D_4$), $0.2902$ ($V_4$), $1.2461$ ($C_4$) against the laws $1$, $1$, $1$, $0.47385$, $1.43018$, $0.29474$, $1.25$; the which-factor walls measure $0.0000$--$0.0001$ bits.

\paragraph{Two estimator traps.} (i) \emph{Sparse-modulus bias}: a plug-in mutual-information estimate over a table with many cells is biased upward by roughly (number of free cells)$/(2n\ln 2)$; for the several-hundred-cell $S_4$ semiprime table a $3\times10^{4}$-draw estimate would carry a bias near $0.10$ bits, enough to fake a violation of the one-bit cap. Raising the draw count to $4\times10^{5}$ puts the bias below the $0.005$-bit resolution of the claims, and permutation nulls confirm residual thickening at the $0.004$-bit level. (ii) \emph{The resolvent shortcut}: reading quartic types from the cubic resolvent is invalid for binomial and other special quartics --- the axis pairing of $x^4-2$ is fixed by all of $D_4$, and for the $V_4$ field the resolvent splits over $\mathbb{Q}$. Types must be computed by genuine factor-degree extraction over $\mathbb{F}_p$, equivalently by counting roots in $\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$.

\section{Discussion and applications}

\subsection{A capacity for arithmetic side channels}

Theorem~A is a budget. If a protocol exposes, per observation, the factorization shape of a fixed polynomial at a prime associated with a secret, the adversary's per-observation yield about the residue class is exactly $I = H(T)-H(T\mid\text{coset}) \le \log_2[G:G']$, computable from a group table of size $\#G$ in time $O(\#G)$. Three design consequences follow: a polynomial with perfect Galois group leaks nothing at all; a polynomial with $G^{\ab}=C_2$ leaks at most one bit per observation regardless of the intricacy of its statistics; and no residue dial that resolves the abelianization is better than any other (Theorem~\ref{thm:law}). Aggregation across the factors of a semiprime does not escape the bound, though a field with a larger abelianization genuinely offers more.

\subsection{A quantitative frontier for reciprocity}

The abelian/non-abelian divide is classically a dichotomy; the law replaces it by a real-valued coordinate:
\[
\underbrace{0}_{\text{perfect } G,\ \text{e.g. } A_5} \;\le\; I \;\le\; \underbrace{H(T)}_{\text{abelian } G}, \qquad I \le \log_2[G:G'] .
\]
Which bound binds is structural: $I = H(T)$ iff the coset determines the type, while $I = \log_2[G:G']$ iff the type determines the coset. The six fields realise three of the four combinations: $S_3$ and $S_4$ attain the cap but not the type entropy; $V_4$ and $C_4$ the type entropy but not the cap; $A_4$ and $D_4$ neither.

\subsection{Unification}

Flatness statements for certain residue channels, criteria for a channel to be nonzero, binary laws for quadratic fields, tabulations for small groups and abelian pair laws at the semiprime level are all projections of Theorem~A. Once the channel is known to equal the abelianization content, each reduces to arithmetic on a finite group table.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{The index-2 rigidity conjecture.} Every field in the table with abelianization $C_2$ attains its cap exactly, while every field with a larger abelianization falls short. For a subgroup of index $2$ the coset readout is the sign of the permutation, and the sign is a function of the cycle type. \emph{Conjecture:} if $[G:G']=2$ and the type readout is the cycle type of a faithful transitive action, then $I=1$ exactly; more generally the channel is complete iff the coset map factors through the cycle-type map, which for a transitive degree-$n$ action happens for every $G$ with $G' \supseteq G\cap A_n$. The completeness criterion has already converted the analytic question into this combinatorial one; what remains needs only $\sign(g) = (-1)^{\,n-\#\text{cycles}(g)}$.

\paragraph{Perfect-group flatness as a theorem about $A_5$.} The general statement is proved; its smallest instance predicts an identically zero channel for an $A_5$ quintic field, for primes and semiprimes alike. Flatness needs no entropy computation: perfection collapses the coset readout to a constant. What remains is the certificate of perfection, most cleanly obtained from the simplicity of $A_5$ rather than from a $60\times60$ commutator census.

\paragraph{The $k$-almost-prime ladder.} The prime and semiprime layers are $k=1,2$ of
\[ I_k = I\big(\text{coset}(g_1\cdots g_k);\ \text{multiset of types}\big). \]
\emph{Conjecture:} $I_k$ is non-increasing in $k$ and tends to $0$ for every field whose abelianization is not an elementary abelian $2$-group, while for $G^{\ab}$ of exponent $2$ it stabilises at a positive limit --- for $S_3$ and $S_4$ at the constant one bit.

\paragraph{Beyond.} Extending the closed forms to degree $5$ and $6$, where the type readout is no longer determined by fixed-point counts; characterising which pairs (group, action) realise a prescribed loss; and studying the channel under conditioning on additional arithmetic data, where the cap still applies but the completeness criterion changes.

\section{Conclusion}

The complete splitting-type channel of a number field is exactly its abelianization content:
\[
I\big(p\bmod m^{*};\,T\big) = I(\text{coset};\,T) = H(T)-H(T\mid\text{coset}) \le \log_2[G:G'],
\]
with equality precisely when the splitting type determines the abelianization coset. At the semiprime level the same law holds verbatim with the class-level type map, and telling the reader which factor carried which shape is worth exactly nothing. Six fields --- $S_3$ twice, $S_4$, $A_4$, $D_4$, with abelian controls $V_4$ and $C_4$ --- are evaluated in exact closed form at both levels, and measurements over real primes reproduce every value. The $S_4$ field shows that the cap sees only the abelianization and not the five splitting types; the $D_4$/$V_4$ pair shows that a non-abelian channel can be strictly richer than an abelian one; and perfect groups, of which $A_5$ is the smallest, are exactly and permanently silent.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from math import gcd, log2
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]  # a permutation of {0, ..., n-1} given by its image tuple

L3 = log2(3.0)
L5 = log2(5.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. A finite uniform channel calculus
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def entropy(values: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """Shannon entropy in bits of the empirical distribution of `values`."""
    counts: Dict[object, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    n = len(values)
    return -sum((c / n) * log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())


def joint_entropy(xs: Sequence[object], ys: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """Shannon entropy in bits of the joint readout (x, y)."""
    return entropy(list(zip(xs, ys)))


def mutual_information(xs: Sequence[object], ys: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """I(X ; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y), in bits."""
    return entropy(xs) + entropy(ys) - joint_entropy(xs, ys)


def conditional_entropy(ys: Sequence[object], xs: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """H(Y | X) = H(X, Y) - H(X), in bits."""
    return joint_entropy(xs, ys) - entropy(xs)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Permutation groups of the roots
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def compose(g: Perm, h: Perm) -> Perm:
    """The permutation (g*h)(x) = g(h(x))."""
    return tuple(g[h[x]] for x in range(len(g)))


def inverse(g: Perm) -> Perm:
    out = [0] * len(g)
    for x, y in enumerate(g):
        out[y] = x
    return tuple(out)


def sign(g: Perm) -> int:
    """+1 for even, -1 for odd permutations."""
    n = len(g)
    seen = [False] * n
    s = 1
    for x in range(n):
        if seen[x]:
            continue
        length = 0
        y = x
        while not seen[y]:
            seen[y] = True
            y = g[y]
            length += 1
        if length % 2 == 0:
            s = -s
    return s


def cycle_type(g: Perm) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """The cycle type of g as a sorted tuple of cycle lengths (the splitting type)."""
    n = len(g)
    seen = [False] * n
    out: List[int] = []
    for x in range(n):
        if seen[x]:
            continue
        length = 0
        y = x
        while not seen[y]:
            seen[y] = True
            y = g[y]
            length += 1
        out.append(length)
    return tuple(sorted(out, reverse=True))


def derived_subgroup(group: Sequence[Perm]) -> List[Perm]:
    """The commutator subgroup [G, G], computed by closure of all commutators."""
    gens = {compose(compose(a, b), compose(inverse(a), inverse(b)))
            for a in group for b in group}
    n = len(group[0])
    closure = {tuple(range(n))}
    frontier = set(gens)
    while frontier:
        new = set()
        for x in frontier:
            if x not in closure:
                closure.add(x)
                for y in list(closure):
                    for z in (compose(x, y), compose(y, x)):
                        if z not in closure:
                            new.add(z)
        frontier = new
    return sorted(closure)


def coset_readout(group: Sequence[Perm], normal: Sequence[Perm]) -> Callable[[Perm], int]:
    """A numeric readout whose level sets are exactly the cosets of `normal` in G.

    This is the abstract form of "the residue class of p modulo the conductor":
    class field theory identifies that residue class with the coset of Frobenius
    modulo the derived subgroup.
    """
    normal_set = set(normal)
    reps: List[Perm] = []
    for g in group:
        if not any(compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set for r in reps):
            reps.append(g)
    index: Dict[Perm, int] = {}
    for g in group:
        for i, r in enumerate(reps):
            if compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set:
                index[g] = i
                break
    return lambda g: index[g]

        assert abs(info - i_form) < 1e-12, (name, info, i_form)
        assert abs(dial - dial_form) < 1e-12, (name, dial, dial_form)
        # decomposition and loss identities
        assert abs(info - (h_type - conditional_entropy(types, cosets))) < 1e-12
        assert abs(loss - conditional_entropy(cosets, types)) < 1e-12
        print(f"{poly:<24}{name:<5}{len(group):>5}{len(group)//len(derived):>9}"
              f"{h_type:>10.5f}{info:>10.5f}{i_form:>10.5f}{loss:>10.5f}")
    print("\nAll six channels match their closed forms exactly, and in every case")
    print("I = H(T) - H(T | coset) and  log2[G:G'] - I = H(coset | T).\n")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Splitting types of honest primes: distinct-degree factorization over F_p
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def poly_trim(a: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    while a and a[-1] == 0:
        a.pop()
    return a


def poly_mulmod(a: List[int], b: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    """(a*b) mod f over F_p, with f monic."""
    out = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1) if a and b else []
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai:
            for j, bj in enumerate(b):
                out[i + j] = (out[i + j] + ai * bj) % p
    return poly_mod(out, f, p)


def poly_mod(a: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a = [x % p for x in a]
    df = len(f) - 1
    while len(a) - 1 >= df and a:
        c = a[-1] % p
        shift = len(a) - 1 - df
        if c:
            for i, fi in enumerate(f):
                a[shift + i] = (a[shift + i] - c * fi) % p
        a.pop()
        poly_trim(a)
    return poly_trim(a)


def poly_gcd(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a = poly_trim([x % p for x in a])
    b = poly_trim([x % p for x in b])
    while b:
        a = poly_mod(a, monic(b, p), p)
        a, b = b, a
    return monic(a, p) if a else a


def monic(a: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    if not a:
        return a
    inv = pow(a[-1], p - 2, p)
    return [(x * inv) % p for x in a]


def poly_powmod(base: List[int], e: int, f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    result = [1]
    b = poly_mod(list(base), f, p)
    while e:
        if e & 1:
            result = poly_mulmod(result, b, f, p)
        b = poly_mulmod(b, b, f, p)
        e >>= 1
    return result


def splitting_type(f: List[int], p: int) -> Tuple[int, ...] | None:
    """The factorization shape of the squarefree polynomial f modulo p.

    Returned as the sorted multiset of the degrees of the irreducible factors, which
    for an unramified prime is exactly the cycle type of Frobenius on the roots.
    Returns None if p is ramified (f mod p is not squarefree) or divides the leading
    coefficient.
    """
    fp = poly_trim([c % p for c in f])
    if len(fp) != len(f):
        return None
    fp = monic(fp, p)
    deriv = poly_trim([(i * c) % p for i, c in enumerate(fp)][1:])
    if not deriv or len(poly_gcd(fp, deriv, p)) > 1:
        return None
    shape: List[int] = []
    current = fp
    d = 0
    while len(current) - 1 > 0:
        d += 1
        if 2 * d > len(current) - 1:
            shape.append(len(current) - 1)
            break
        h = poly_powmod([0, 1], p ** d, current, p)   # x^(p^d) mod current
        hx = poly_trim([(hi - (1 if i == 1 else 0)) % p
                        for i, hi in enumerate(h + [0] * max(0, 2 - len(h)))])
        g = poly_gcd(hx, current, p) if hx else list(current)
        # g = gcd(x^(p^d) - x, current): product of the irreducible factors of degree d
        if len(g) - 1 > 0:
            shape.extend([d] * ((len(g) - 1) // d))
            current = monic(poly_mod_div(current, g, p), p)
    return tuple(sorted(shape, reverse=True))


def poly_mod_div(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    """Exact quotient a / b over F_p (b assumed to divide a)."""
    a = list(a)
    q = [0] * (len(a) - len(b) + 1)
    binv = pow(b[-1], p - 2, p)
    for shift in range(len(a) - len(b), -1, -1):
        c = (a[shift + len(b) - 1] * binv) % p
        q[shift] = c
        if c:
            for i, bi in enumerate(b):
                a[shift + i] = (a[shift + i] - c * bi) % p
    return poly_trim(q)


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):
                sieve[j] = False
    return [i for i, ok in enumerate(sieve) if ok]


def legendre(a: int, p: int) -> int:
    a %= p
    if a == 0:
        return 0
    return 1 if pow(a, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1 else -1


def empirical_channels(bound: int = 60000) -> None:
    print("=" * 88)
    print(f"(3) EMPIRICAL PRIME-LEVEL CHANNELS (primes up to {bound})")
    print("=" * 88)
    ps = [p for p in primes_up_to(bound) if p > 3]

    # (polynomial coefficients low-to-high, name, residue dial, closed-form I)
    experiments: List[Tuple[str, List[int], str, Callable[[int], int], float]] = [
        ("x^3 + x + 1", [1, 1, 0, 1], "S3", lambda p: legendre(-31, p), 1.0),
        ("x^3 - x + 1", [1, -1, 0, 1], "S3", lambda p: legendre(-23, p), 1.0),
        ("x^4 - x - 1", [-1, -1, 0, 0, 1], "S4", lambda p: legendre(-283, p), 1.0),
        ("x^4 - 2", [-2, 0, 0, 0, 1], "D4", lambda p: p % 8, 9 / 4 - 3 * L3 / 8),
        ("Phi_5", [1, 1, 1, 1, 1], "C4", lambda p: p % 5, 3 / 2),
    ]
    header = f"{'field':<16}{'G':<5}{'#primes':>9}{'H(T)':>10}{'I measured':>12}{'law':>10}{'|diff|':>9}"
    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))
    for poly_name, coeffs, group_name, dial, law in experiments:
        types: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
        dials: List[int] = []
        for p in ps:
            t = splitting_type(coeffs, p)
            if t is None:
                continue
            types.append(t)
            dials.append(dial(p))
        info = mutual_information(dials, types)
        print(f"{poly_name:<16}{group_name:<5}{len(types):>9}{entropy(types):>10.5f}"
              f"{info:>12.5f}{law:>10.5f}{abs(info - law):>9.5f}")
    print("\nThe measured channels of honest primes sit on the group-theoretic law to")
    print("within finite-sample noise; the residue dial never learns more about the")
    print("factorization shape than the abelianization coset already knows.\n")

# 6. Structural phenomena: the cap, the reversal, and perfect-group flatness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def structural_phenomena() -> None:
    print("=" * 88)
    print("(4) STRUCTURAL PHENOMENA")
    print("=" * 88)

    # The S4 cap: five types, more than two bits of type entropy, exactly one bit out.
    types_s4 = [cycle_type(g) for g in S4]
    coset_s4 = coset_readout(S4, derived_subgroup(S4))
    i_s4 = mutual_information([coset_s4(g) for g in S4], types_s4)
    print(f"S4: {len(set(types_s4))} distinct splitting types, H(T) = {entropy(types_s4):.5f} bits,")
    print(f"    channel = {i_s4:.5f} bit.  The cap log2 [S4 : A4] = 1 is a statement about the")
    print("    abelianization, not about the number of types.")

    # The reversal.
    i_v4 = mutual_information([coset_readout(V4, derived_subgroup(V4))(g) for g in V4],
                              [cycle_type(g) for g in V4])
    i_d4 = mutual_information([coset_readout(D4, derived_subgroup(D4))(g) for g in D4],
                              [cycle_type(g) for g in D4])
    print(f"\nReversal: abelian V4 channel = {i_v4:.5f} < non-abelian D4 channel = {i_d4:.5f},")
    print("    both under the same two-bit cap.  Richness is decided by how well the readout")
    print("    separates cosets, not by whether the group is abelian.")
    assert i_v4 < i_d4

    # Completeness criterion, field by field.
    print("\nCompleteness criterion (channel attains the cap iff the type determines the coset):")
    for poly, name, group in FIELDS:
        coset = coset_readout(group, derived_subgroup(group))
        determines = True
        by_type: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {}
        for g in group:
            t = cycle_type(g)
            if t in by_type and by_type[t] != coset(g):
                determines = False
            by_type.setdefault(t, coset(g))
        dial = log2(len(group) // len(derived_subgroup(group)))
        info = mutual_information([coset(g) for g in group], [cycle_type(g) for g in group])
        complete = abs(info - dial) < 1e-12
        assert determines == complete
        print(f"    {name:<3} type determines coset: {str(determines):<5}  "
              f"channel attains cap: {str(complete):<5}  loss = {dial - info:.5f}")

    # Perfect group flatness: A5.
    A5 = [g for g in (tuple(p) for p in permutations(range(5))) if sign(g) == 1]
    derived_a5 = derived_subgroup(A5)
    coset_a5 = coset_readout(A5, derived_a5)
    i_a5 = mutual_information([coset_a5(g) for g in A5], [cycle_type(g) for g in A5])
    print(f"\nPerfect group: |A5| = {len(A5)}, |[A5, A5]| = {len(derived_a5)}, so the coset readout")
    print(f"    is constant and the channel is exactly {i_a5:.5f} bits: an A5 field's splitting")
    print("    statistics are statistically independent of every residue dial.")
    assert abs(i_a5) < 1e-12


def main() -> None:
    prime_level_table()
    semiprime_table()
    empirical_channels()
    structural_phenomena()
    print("=" * 88)
    print("All assertions passed.")
    print("=" * 88)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from math import gcd, log2
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]  # a permutation of {0, ..., n-1} given by its image tuple

L3 = log2(3.0)
L5 = log2(5.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. A finite uniform channel calculus
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def entropy(values: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """Shannon entropy in bits of the empirical distribution of `values`."""
    counts: Dict[object, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    n = len(values)
    return -sum((c / n) * log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())


def joint_entropy(xs: Sequence[object], ys: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """Shannon entropy in bits of the joint readout (x, y)."""
    return entropy(list(zip(xs, ys)))


def mutual_information(xs: Sequence[object], ys: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """I(X ; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y), in bits."""
    return entropy(xs) + entropy(ys) - joint_entropy(xs, ys)


def conditional_entropy(ys: Sequence[object], xs: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    """H(Y | X) = H(X, Y) - H(X), in bits."""
    return joint_entropy(xs, ys) - entropy(xs)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Permutation groups of the roots
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def compose(g: Perm, h: Perm) -> Perm:
    """The permutation (g*h)(x) = g(h(x))."""
    return tuple(g[h[x]] for x in range(len(g)))


def inverse(g: Perm) -> Perm:
    out = [0] * len(g)
    for x, y in enumerate(g):
        out[y] = x
    return tuple(out)


def sign(g: Perm) -> int:
    """+1 for even, -1 for odd permutations."""
    n = len(g)
    seen = [False] * n
    s = 1
    for x in range(n):
        if seen[x]:
            continue
        length = 0
        y = x
        while not seen[y]:
            seen[y] = True
            y = g[y]
            length += 1
        if length % 2 == 0:
            s = -s
    return s


def cycle_type(g: Perm) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """The cycle type of g as a sorted tuple of cycle lengths (the splitting type)."""
    n = len(g)
    seen = [False] * n
    out: List[int] = []
    for x in range(n):
        if seen[x]:
            continue
        length = 0
        y = x
        while not seen[y]:
            seen[y] = True
            y = g[y]
            length += 1
        out.append(length)
    return tuple(sorted(out, reverse=True))


def derived_subgroup(group: Sequence[Perm]) -> List[Perm]:
    """The commutator subgroup [G, G], computed by closure of all commutators."""
    gens = {compose(compose(a, b), compose(inverse(a), inverse(b)))
            for a in group for b in group}
    n = len(group[0])
    closure = {tuple(range(n))}
    frontier = set(gens)
    while frontier:
        new = set()
        for x in frontier:
            if x not in closure:
                closure.add(x)
                for y in list(closure):
                    for z in (compose(x, y), compose(y, x)):
                        if z not in closure:
                            new.add(z)
        frontier = new
    return sorted(closure)


def coset_readout(group: Sequence[Perm], normal: Sequence[Perm]) -> Callable[[Perm], int]:
    """A numeric readout whose level sets are exactly the cosets of `normal` in G.

    This is the abstract form of "the residue class of p modulo the conductor":
    class field theory identifies that residue class with the coset of Frobenius
    modulo the derived subgroup.
    """
    normal_set = set(normal)
    reps: List[Perm] = []
    for g in group:
        if not any(compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set for r in reps):
            reps.append(g)
    index: Dict[Perm, int] = {}
    for g in group:
        for i, r in enumerate(reps):
            if compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set:
                index[g] = i
                break
    return lambda g: index[g]


# The six Galois groups of the experiment, as permutation groups of the roots.

S3: List[Perm] = [tuple(p) for p in permutations(range(3))]

D4: List[Perm] = [g for g in S4 if {g[0], g[2]} in ({0, 2}, {1, 3})]

C4: List[Perm] = [g for g in S4 if g[1] == (g[0] + 1) % 4 and g[2] == (g[0] + 2) % 4

# 5. Splitting types of honest primes: distinct-degree factorization over F_p
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def poly_trim(a: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    while a and a[-1] == 0:
        a.pop()
    return a


def poly_mulmod(a: List[int], b: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    """(a*b) mod f over F_p, with f monic."""
    out = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1) if a and b else []
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai:
            for j, bj in enumerate(b):
                out[i + j] = (out[i + j] + ai * bj) % p
    return poly_mod(out, f, p)


def poly_mod(a: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a = [x % p for x in a]
    df = len(f) - 1
    while len(a) - 1 >= df and a:
        c = a[-1] % p
        shift = len(a) - 1 - df
        if c:
            for i, fi in enumerate(f):
                a[shift + i] = (a[shift + i] - c * fi) % p
        a.pop()
        poly_trim(a)
    return poly_trim(a)


def poly_gcd(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a = poly_trim([x % p for x in a])
    b = poly_trim([x % p for x in b])
    while b:
        a = poly_mod(a, monic(b, p), p)
        a, b = b, a
    return monic(a, p) if a else a


def monic(a: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    if not a:
        return a
    inv = pow(a[-1], p - 2, p)
    return [(x * inv) % p for x in a]


def poly_powmod(base: List[int], e: int, f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    result = [1]
    b = poly_mod(list(base), f, p)
    while e:
        if e & 1:
            result = poly_mulmod(result, b, f, p)
        b = poly_mulmod(b, b, f, p)
        e >>= 1
    return result


def splitting_type(f: List[int], p: int) -> Tuple[int, ...] | None:
    """The factorization shape of the squarefree polynomial f modulo p.

    Returned as the sorted multiset of the degrees of the irreducible factors, which
    for an unramified prime is exactly the cycle type of Frobenius on the roots.
    Returns None if p is ramified (f mod p is not squarefree) or divides the leading
    coefficient.
    """
    fp = poly_trim([c % p for c in f])
    if len(fp) != len(f):
        return None
    fp = monic(fp, p)
    deriv = poly_trim([(i * c) % p for i, c in enumerate(fp)][1:])
    if not deriv or len(poly_gcd(fp, deriv, p)) > 1:
        return None
    shape: List[int] = []
    current = fp
    d = 0
    while len(current) - 1 > 0:
        d += 1
        if 2 * d > len(current) - 1:
            shape.append(len(current) - 1)
            break
        h = poly_powmod([0, 1], p ** d, current, p)   # x^(p^d) mod current
        hx = poly_trim([(hi - (1 if i == 1 else 0)) % p
                        for i, hi in enumerate(h + [0] * max(0, 2 - len(h)))])
        g = poly_gcd(hx, current, p) if hx else list(current)
        # g = gcd(x^(p^d) - x, current): product of the irreducible factors of degree d
        if len(g) - 1 > 0:
            shape.extend([d] * ((len(g) - 1) // d))
            current = monic(poly_mod_div(current, g, p), p)
    return tuple(sorted(shape, reverse=True))


def poly_mod_div(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    """Exact quotient a / b over F_p (b assumed to divide a)."""
    a = list(a)
    q = [0] * (len(a) - len(b) + 1)
    binv = pow(b[-1], p - 2, p)
    for shift in range(len(a) - len(b), -1, -1):
        c = (a[shift + len(b) - 1] * binv) % p
        q[shift] = c
        if c:
            for i, bi in enumerate(b):
                a[shift + i] = (a[shift + i] - c * bi) % p
    return poly_trim(q)


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):
                sieve[j] = False
    return [i for i, ok in enumerate(sieve) if ok]


def legendre(a: int, p: int) -> int:
    a %= p
    if a == 0:
        return 0
    return 1 if pow(a, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1 else -1

def structural_phenomena() -> None:
    print("=" * 88)
    print("(4) STRUCTURAL PHENOMENA")

    # The S4 cap: five types, more than two bits of type entropy, exactly one bit out.

    print(f"    channel = {i_s4:.5f} bit.  The cap log2 [S4 : A4] = 1 is a statement about the")
    print("    abelianization, not about the number of types.")

    # The reversal.
    i_v4 = mutual_information([coset_readout(V4, derived_subgroup(V4))(g) for g in V4],
                              [cycle_type(g) for g in V4])
    i_d4 = mutual_information([coset_readout(D4, derived_subgroup(D4))(g) for g in D4],
                              [cycle_type(g) for g in D4])
    print(f"\nReversal: abelian V4 channel = {i_v4:.5f} < non-abelian D4 channel = {i_d4:.5f},")
    print("    both under the same two-bit cap.  Richness is decided by how well the readout")
    print("    separates cosets, not by whether the group is abelian.")
    assert i_v4 < i_d4

    # Completeness criterion, field by field.
    print("\nCompleteness criterion (channel attains the cap iff the type determines the coset):")
    for poly, name, group in FIELDS:
        coset = coset_readout(group, derived_subgroup(group))
        determines = True
        by_type: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {}
        for g in group:
            t = cycle_type(g)
            if t in by_type and by_type[t] != coset(g):
                determines = False
            by_type.setdefault(t, coset(g))
        dial = log2(len(group) // len(derived_subgroup(group)))
        info = mutual_information([coset(g) for g in group], [cycle_type(g) for g in group])
        complete = abs(info - dial) < 1e-12
        assert determines == complete
        print(f"    {name:<3} type determines coset: {str(determines):<5}  "
              f"channel attains cap: {str(complete):<5}  loss = {dial - info:.5f}")

    # Perfect group flatness: A5.
    A5 = [g for g in (tuple(p) for p in permutations(range(5))) if sign(g) == 1]
    derived_a5 = derived_subgroup(A5)
    coset_a5 = coset_readout(A5, derived_a5)
    i_a5 = mutual_information([coset_a5(g) for g in A5], [cycle_type(g) for g in A5])
    print(f"\nPerfect group: |A5| = {len(A5)}, |[A5, A5]| = {len(derived_a5)}, so the coset readout")
    print(f"    is constant and the channel is exactly {i_a5:.5f} bits: an A5 field's splitting")
    print("    statistics are statistically independent of every residue dial.")
    assert abs(i_a5) < 1e-12

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from math import log2
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


def compose(g: Perm, h: Perm) -> Perm:
    return tuple(g[h[x]] for x in range(len(g)))


def inverse(g: Perm) -> Perm:
    out = [0] * len(g)
    for x, y in enumerate(g):
        out[y] = x
    return tuple(out)


def cycle_type(g: Perm) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    seen = [False] * len(g)
    out: List[int] = []
    for x in range(len(g)):
        if seen[x]:
            continue
        length, y = 0, x
        while not seen[y]:
            seen[y] = True
            y = g[y]
            length += 1
        out.append(length)
    return tuple(sorted(out, reverse=True))


def is_even(g: Perm) -> bool:
    return sum(length - 1 for length in cycle_type(g)) % 2 == 0


def entropy(values: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    counts: Dict[object, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    n = len(values)
    return -sum((c / n) * log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())


def mutual_information(xs: Sequence[object], ys: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    return entropy(xs) + entropy(ys) - entropy(list(zip(xs, ys)))


def derived_subgroup(group: Sequence[Perm]) -> List[Perm]:
    identity = tuple(range(len(group[0])))
    closure = {identity}
    frontier = {compose(compose(a, b), compose(inverse(a), inverse(b)))
                for a in group for b in group}
    while frontier:
        new = set()
        for x in frontier:
            if x in closure:
                continue
            closure.add(x)
            for y in list(closure):
                for z in (compose(x, y), compose(y, x)):
                    if z not in closure:
                        new.add(z)
        frontier = new
    return sorted(closure)


def coset_index(group: Sequence[Perm], normal: Sequence[Perm]) -> Dict[Perm, int]:
    normal_set = set(normal)
    reps: List[Perm] = []
    for g in group:
        if not any(compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set for r in reps):
            reps.append(g)
    return {g: next(i for i, r in enumerate(reps) if compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set)
            for g in group}


def report(name: str, group: Sequence[Perm]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    normal = derived_subgroup(group)
    idx = coset_index(group, normal)
    types = [cycle_type(g) for g in group]
    cosets = [idx[g] for g in group]
    h_t = entropy(types)
    info = mutual_information(cosets, types)
    cap = log2(len(group) // len(normal))
    determines = len({(t, c) for t, c in zip(types, cosets)}) == len(set(types))

          f"loss = {cap - info:7.5f}   type determines coset: {determines}")
    return h_t, info, cap

def compose(g: Perm, h: Perm) -> Perm:

    seen = [False] * len(g)

    for x in range(len(g)):

        while not seen[y]:

            length += 1
        out.append(length)
    return tuple(sorted(out, reverse=True))


def derived_subgroup(group: Sequence[Perm]) -> List[Perm]:
    """[G, G]: the subgroup generated by all commutators a b a^-1 b^-1."""
    identity = tuple(range(len(group[0])))
    closure = {identity}
    frontier = {compose(compose(a, b), compose(inverse(a), inverse(b)))
                for a in group for b in group}
    while frontier:
        new = set()
        for x in frontier:
            if x in closure:
                continue
            closure.add(x)
            for y in list(closure):
                for z in (compose(x, y), compose(y, x)):
                    if z not in closure:
                        new.add(z)
        frontier = new
    return sorted(closure)


def coset_readout(group: Sequence[Perm], normal: Sequence[Perm]) -> Callable[[Perm], int]:
    """A numeric readout whose level sets are exactly the cosets of `normal`."""
    normal_set = set(normal)
    reps: List[Perm] = []
    for g in group:
        if not any(compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set for r in reps):
            reps.append(g)
    index = {g: next(i for i, r in enumerate(reps) if compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set)

    return lambda g: index[g]

    counts: Dict[object, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    n = len(values)
    return -sum((c / n) * log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Optional, Tuple


def poly_trim(a: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    while a and a[-1] == 0:
        a.pop()
    return a


def monic(a: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    if not a:
        return a
    inv = pow(a[-1], p - 2, p)
    return [(x * inv) % p for x in a]


def poly_mod(a: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    """Remainder of a modulo the monic polynomial f, over F_p."""
    a = [x % p for x in a]
    df = len(f) - 1
    while a and len(a) - 1 >= df:
        c = a[-1] % p
        shift = len(a) - 1 - df
        if c:
            for i, fi in enumerate(f):
                a[shift + i] = (a[shift + i] - c * fi) % p
        a.pop()
        poly_trim(a)
    return poly_trim(a)


def poly_mulmod(a: List[int], b: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    out = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1) if a and b else []
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai:
            for j, bj in enumerate(b):
                out[i + j] = (out[i + j] + ai * bj) % p
    return poly_mod(out, f, p)


def poly_powmod(base: List[int], e: int, f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    result, b = [1], poly_mod(list(base), f, p)
    while e:
        if e & 1:
            result = poly_mulmod(result, b, f, p)
        b = poly_mulmod(b, b, f, p)
        e >>= 1
    return result


def poly_gcd(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a, b = poly_trim([x % p for x in a]), poly_trim([x % p for x in b])
    while b:
        a = poly_mod(a, monic(b, p), p)
        a, b = b, a
    return monic(a, p) if a else a


def poly_exact_div(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a = list(a)
    q = [0] * (len(a) - len(b) + 1)
    binv = pow(b[-1], p - 2, p)
    for shift in range(len(a) - len(b), -1, -1):
        c = (a[shift + len(b) - 1] * binv) % p
        q[shift] = c
        if c:
            for i, bi in enumerate(b):
                a[shift + i] = (a[shift + i] - c * bi) % p
    return poly_trim(q)


def splitting_type(coeffs: List[int], p: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """The factorization shape of f mod p (coefficients given low-to-high).

    Returns the sorted multiset of factor degrees, or None if p is ramified
    (f mod p not squarefree) or divides the leading coefficient.
    """
    fp = poly_trim([c % p for c in coeffs])
    if len(fp) != len(coeffs):
        return None
    fp = monic(fp, p)
    deriv = poly_trim([(i * c) % p for i, c in enumerate(fp)][1:])
    if not deriv or len(poly_gcd(fp, deriv, p)) > 1:
        return None
    shape: List[int] = []
    current, d = fp, 0
    while len(current) - 1 > 0:
        d += 1
        if 2 * d > len(current) - 1:           # what remains must be irreducible
            shape.append(len(current) - 1)
            break
        h = poly_powmod([0, 1], p ** d, current, p)          # x^(p^d) mod current
        hx = poly_trim([(hi - (1 if i == 1 else 0)) % p
                        for i, hi in enumerate(h + [0] * max(0, 2 - len(h)))])
        g = poly_gcd(hx, current, p) if hx else list(current)
        if len(g) - 1 > 0:
            shape.extend([d] * ((len(g) - 1) // d))
            current = monic(poly_exact_div(current, g, p), p)
    return tuple(sorted(shape, reverse=True))

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from math import log2
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


def compose(g: Perm, h: Perm) -> Perm:
    return tuple(g[h[x]] for x in range(len(g)))


def inverse(g: Perm) -> Perm:
    out = [0] * len(g)
    for x, y in enumerate(g):
        out[y] = x
    return tuple(out)


def cycle_type(g: Perm) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    seen = [False] * len(g)
    out: List[int] = []
    for x in range(len(g)):
        if seen[x]:
            continue
        length, y = 0, x
        while not seen[y]:
            seen[y] = True
            y = g[y]
            length += 1
        out.append(length)
    return tuple(sorted(out, reverse=True))


def entropy(values: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    counts: Dict[object, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    n = len(values)
    return -sum((c / n) * log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())


def mutual_information(xs: Sequence[object], ys: Sequence[object]) -> float:
    return entropy(xs) + entropy(ys) - entropy(list(zip(xs, ys)))


def derived_subgroup(group: Sequence[Perm]) -> List[Perm]:
    identity = tuple(range(len(group[0])))
    closure = {identity}
    frontier = {compose(compose(a, b), compose(inverse(a), inverse(b)))
                for a in group for b in group}
    while frontier:
        new = set()
        for x in frontier:
            if x in closure:
                continue
            closure.add(x)
            for y in list(closure):
                for z in (compose(x, y), compose(y, x)):
                    if z not in closure:
                        new.add(z)
        frontier = new
    return sorted(closure)


def coset_index(group: Sequence[Perm], normal: Sequence[Perm]) -> Dict[Perm, int]:
    normal_set = set(normal)
    reps: List[Perm] = []
    for g in group:
        if not any(compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set for r in reps):
            reps.append(g)
    return {g: next(i for i, r in enumerate(reps) if compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set)
            for g in group}


def semiprime_channel(group: Sequence[Perm]) -> Dict[str, float]:
    normal = derived_subgroup(group)
    idx = coset_index(group, normal)
    pairs = list(product(group, group))
    prod_coset = [idx[compose(x, y)] for x, y in pairs]
    unordered = [tuple(sorted((cycle_type(x), cycle_type(y)))) for x, y in pairs]
    ordered = [(cycle_type(x), cycle_type(y)) for x, y in pairs]
    i2 = mutual_information(prod_coset, unordered)
    i2_ord = mutual_information(prod_coset, ordered)
    return {"I2": i2, "I2_ordered": i2_ord, "which_factor_wall": abs(i2 - i2_ord),
            "cap": log2(len(group) // len(normal))}

def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)

        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):

    return [i for i, ok in enumerate(sieve) if ok]


def poly_trim(a: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    while a and a[-1] == 0:
        a.pop()
    return a


def monic(a: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    if not a:
        return a
    inv = pow(a[-1], p - 2, p)
    return [(x * inv) % p for x in a]


def poly_mod(a: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a = [x % p for x in a]
    df = len(f) - 1
    while a and len(a) - 1 >= df:
        c = a[-1] % p
        shift = len(a) - 1 - df
        if c:
            for i, fi in enumerate(f):
                a[shift + i] = (a[shift + i] - c * fi) % p
        a.pop()
        poly_trim(a)
    return poly_trim(a)


def poly_mulmod(a: List[int], b: List[int], f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    out = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1) if a and b else []
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai:
            for j, bj in enumerate(b):
                out[i + j] = (out[i + j] + ai * bj) % p
    return poly_mod(out, f, p)


def poly_powmod(base: List[int], e: int, f: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    result, b = [1], poly_mod(list(base), f, p)
    while e:
        if e & 1:
            result = poly_mulmod(result, b, f, p)
        b = poly_mulmod(b, b, f, p)
        e >>= 1
    return result


def poly_gcd(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:
    a, b = poly_trim([x % p for x in a]), poly_trim([x % p for x in b])
    while b:
        a = poly_mod(a, monic(b, p), p)
        a, b = b, a
    return monic(a, p) if a else a


def poly_exact_div(a: List[int], b: List[int], p: int) -> List[int]:

        q[shift] = c
        if c:
            for i, bi in enumerate(b):

    return poly_trim(q)

    current, d = fp, 0

    return entropy(xs) + entropy(ys) - entropy(list(zip(xs, ys)))

def compose(g: Perm, h: Perm) -> Perm:
    return tuple(g[h[x]] for x in range(len(g)))


def inverse(g: Perm) -> Perm:
    out = [0] * len(g)
    for x, y in enumerate(g):
        out[y] = x
    return tuple(out)


def cycle_type(g: Perm) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    seen = [False] * len(g)
    out: List[int] = []
    for x in range(len(g)):
        if seen[x]:
            continue
        length, y = 0, x
        while not seen[y]:
            seen[y] = True
            y = g[y]
            length += 1
        out.append(length)
    return tuple(sorted(out, reverse=True))


def sign(g: Perm) -> int:
    return int(np.prod([1 if length % 2 else -1 for length in cycle_type(g)]))


def derived_subgroup(group: Sequence[Perm]) -> List[Perm]:
    identity = tuple(range(len(group[0])))
    closure = {identity}
    frontier = {compose(compose(a, b), compose(inverse(a), inverse(b)))
                for a in group for b in group}
    while frontier:
        new = set()
        for x in frontier:
            if x in closure:
                continue
            closure.add(x)
            for y in list(closure):
                for z in (compose(x, y), compose(y, x)):
                    if z not in closure:
                        new.add(z)
        frontier = new
    return sorted(closure)


def coset_index(group: Sequence[Perm], normal: Sequence[Perm]) -> Dict[Perm, int]:
    normal_set = set(normal)
    reps: List[Perm] = []
    for g in group:
        if not any(compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set for r in reps):
            reps.append(g)
    return {g: next(i for i, r in enumerate(reps) if compose(g, inverse(r)) in normal_set)
            for g in group}


S4 = [tuple(p) for p in permutations(range(4))]
GROUPS: List[Tuple[str, List[Perm]]] = [
    ("$S_3$  ($x^3+x+1$)", [tuple(p) for p in permutations(range(3))]),

*A guided tour of the type-channel law: the exact number of bits that the residue class of a prime carries about the way a polynomial factors.*

---

## 1. The oldest secret in number theory

Take the polynomial $x^2 + 1$. Modulo $5$ it factors as $(x-2)(x+2)$; modulo $7$ it stays irreducible. Which happens is not a mystery: $x^2+1$ splits modulo $p$ exactly when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. Knowing $p$ modulo $4$ tells you the factorization shape, and the shape tells you $p$ modulo $4$. Information flows both ways, losslessly. This is **quadratic reciprocity**, the prototype of [class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory).

Now take $x^3 + x + 1$. There is **no modulus whatsoever** for which $p \bmod m$ determines how this cubic factors. This is the frontier where abelian reciprocity stops. And yet something clearly leaks: whether the cubic has a repeated pattern of linear factors is tied to whether $-31$ is a square modulo $p$.

So the honest question is not "does the residue class determine the shape?" but **"how many bits does it carry?"** — and that question has an exact answer.

> **The Type-Channel Law.** For a polynomial whose splitting field has Galois group $G$ with commutator subgroup $G' = [G,G]$,
> $$I(\text{residue class of } p \;;\; \text{splitting type of } p) \;=\; I(\text{abelianization coset}\;;\;\text{type}) \;=\; H(T) - H(T \mid \text{coset}) \;\le\; \log_2 [G:G'] .$$

Everything below unpacks that sentence, and lets you compute it yourself.

<details>
<summary><b>Background: what is a splitting type, and what is Frobenius?</b> (click to expand)</summary>

Fix a monic irreducible $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree $n$ and a prime $p$ not dividing $\mathrm{disc}(f)$. Over $\mathbb{F}_p$, the reduction $f \bmod p$ factors into distinct irreducible pieces; the multiset of their degrees is the **splitting type** $T(p)$. For a cubic the options are $[1,1,1]$, $[2,1]$, $[3]$; for a quartic, $[1,1,1,1]$, $[2,1,1]$, $[2,2]$, $[3,1]$, $[4]$.

The Galois group $G$ of the splitting field permutes the $n$ roots, so $G \le S_n$. To each unramified prime is attached a conjugacy class in $G$, the [Frobenius class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_endomorphism), and the splitting type of $p$ is exactly the *cycle type* of that class. Two classical facts turn arithmetic into finite group theory:

* **[Chebotarev's density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev%27s_density_theorem) (1922):** as $p$ varies, Frobenius is equidistributed over $G$. So statistics of primes are statistics of a uniformly random group element.
* **Class field theory:** the residue class of $p$ modulo the right conductor sees exactly one thing about Frobenius — its coset modulo the commutator subgroup $G'$. Nothing more.

Those two facts are the entire bridge. Everything afterwards is a computation on a finite group of size at most a few dozen.
</details>

---

## 2. Measuring the leak in bits

Information theory supplies the instrument. For two readouts $X$ and $Y$ of the same random object,
$$H(X) = -\sum_x \Pr[X=x] \log_2 \Pr[X=x], \qquad I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y).$$
The mutual information $I(X;Y)$ is zero exactly when the readouts are independent and equals $H(X)$ exactly when $Y$ determines $X$.

Applied here: put the uniform measure on $G$; let $T(g)$ be the cycle type and $c(g)$ the coset of $g$ modulo $G'$. Then $I(c;T)$ is the exact capacity, in bits per prime, of the channel from arithmetic progressions to factorization shapes.

Two elementary facts do most of the work.

<details>
<summary><b>The two inequalities behind everything</b></summary>

**Lagrange, channel form.** If $c$ is a coset readout for a subgroup $N$, every fibre of $c$ is a coset of $N$ and has the same size $\#N$. A readout with equally sized fibres and $m$ values has entropy $\log_2 m$, so $H(c) = \log_2[G:N]$.

**The cap.** Mutual information never exceeds the entropy of either readout, so
$$I(c;T) \le H(c) = \log_2[G:G'] .$$
This bound is blind to the number of splitting types and to $H(T)$: it depends only on the abelianization.

**Gibbs.** $I(c;T) \ge 0$, by applying $\log t \le t-1$ cellwise to the ratio of the product distribution to the joint distribution.

Combining, the shortfall from the cap has an exact meaning:
$$\log_2[G:G'] - I(c;T) = H(c \mid T),$$
the residual uncertainty about the residue class once the splitting shape is known. That is the "loss" column of every table below.
</details>

## 3. Play with the channel yourself

Here is the whole theory in one interactive object. Choose a Galois group and read the joint table: rows are splitting types, columns are residue classes, each cell counts the group elements of that type in that class. Then watch the bar chart of bits.

Three experiments worth doing:

1. Choose **$S_4$** ($x^4-x-1$). It has five splitting types and over two bits of splitting entropy, yet the channel is exactly **one bit** — the cap of its $C_2$ abelianization. Notice that every row lives in a single column: the type determines the class, so the channel is *complete*.
2. Choose **$A_4$**. Now the type $[3,1]$ straddles two columns. The channel falls short of its cap by exactly $2/3$ of a bit.
3. Choose **$A_5$**, a perfect group. There is only one column. The channel is exactly zero.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why "a row in a single column" is the whole criterion</b></summary>

**Determinism criterion.** On a finite uniform sample space, $H(g \mid f) = 0$ if and only if $f$ determines $g$ pointwise.

*Proof.* Write the conditional entropy as a sum over the cells of the joint table:
$$H(g\mid f) = \sum_{a,b}\Big(P(a,b)\log_2 P_1(a) - P(a,b)\log_2 P(a,b)\Big),$$
where $P$ is the joint distribution and $P_1$ the marginal of $f$. Each summand is $\ge 0$, since $0 < P(a,b) \le P_1(a)$ for nonempty cells and $\log_2$ is increasing. Strict monotonicity of $\log_2$ makes a summand vanish *only* when the cell is empty or when it exhausts its entire row. So the total vanishes precisely when each row of the table is concentrated in a single column — which is exactly determinism. $\blacksquare$

**Completeness criterion.** Therefore $I(c;T) = \log_2[G:G']$ **iff** the splitting type determines the abelianization coset. An analytic question about capacity becomes a combinatorial question about a factorisation of maps — which is why the widget above can answer it by eye.

Two immediate corollaries bound the spectrum:
* **Abelian $G$:** $G' = 1$, the coset readout is injective, and $I = H(T)$ for *every* readout. This is reciprocity.
* **Perfect $G$ (i.e. $G' = G$):** there is one coset, the readout is constant, and $I = 0$ identically.
</details>

## 5. The reversal: abelian does not mean rich

Look at the $V_4$ and $D_4$ rows again.

* $V_4$ is **abelian**, indeed its own abelianization, so its cap is the full $2$ bits. But all three of its non-identity elements are double transpositions with the same splitting type $[2,2]$, so three of its four residue classes look identical to the type reader. Channel: $0.81128$ bits.
* $D_4$ is **non-abelian**, with a smaller relative abelianization. But its type readout separates its cosets far better. Channel: $1.65564$ bits.

$$I(V_4) \approx 0.81128 \;<\; I(D_4) \approx 1.65564 .$$

The non-abelian field leaks more than twice as much per prime as the abelian one. **Richness is decided by how well the readout separates the cosets, not by whether the group is abelian.** Abelianness sets the ceiling; separation decides how much of the ceiling is used.

{{demo:1}}

## 6. Semiprimes: multiplying the secret

Cryptography rarely hands you a prime. It hands you $N = pq$. Such a reader sees the residue of $N$ — corresponding to the *product* of the two Frobenius cosets — and the **unordered** pair of splitting shapes. Modelling the two Frobenius elements as independent uniform elements of $G$, the semiprime channel is
$$I_2 = I\big(c(xy)\;;\;\{T(x), T(y)\}\big).$$

| Field | $G$ | $I_2$ | numerically |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x^3\pm x+1$ | $S_3$ | $1$ | $1.00000$ |
| $x^4-x-1$ | $S_4$ | $1$ | $1.00000$ |
| $x^4+8x+12$ | $A_4$ | $L_3 - \tfrac{10}{9}$ | $0.47385$ |
| $x^4-2$ | $D_4$ | $\tfrac{39}{16}-\tfrac34 L_3 + \tfrac{5}{64}\log_2 5$ | $1.43018$ |
| $x^4-2x^2+9$ | $V_4$ | $\tfrac{19}{8}-\tfrac{21}{16}L_3$ | $0.29474$ |
| $\Phi_5$ | $C_4$ | $\tfrac54$ | $1.25000$ |

Three things survive the passage to products: the $C_2$ cap (the five-type $S_4$ field still yields exactly one bit), the reversal (the non-abelian $D_4$ now exceeds *every* quadratic field, at $1.43018$ bits), and a wall.

> **The Which-Factor Wall.** Telling the reader which prime factor carried which splitting shape is worth exactly **zero** bits. Replacing the unordered pair by the ordered pair leaves $I_2$ unchanged, in every field.

Explore this yourself — change the group and watch the two numbers stay locked together:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why the wall is not a coincidence</b></summary>

The coset of the product $xy$ is a symmetric function of the pair $(x,y)$. The extra data in the ordered readout — which factor is which — is exactly the antisymmetric part, and it is independent of a symmetric statistic once the multiset is known. Formally, the ordered and unordered type entropies differ by precisely the amount by which the corresponding joint entropies differ, so the difference cancels in $I = H(c) + H(\text{type}) - H(\text{joint})$.
</details>

## 7. Do honest primes obey the law?

The closed forms are statements about uniform measures on finite groups; their arithmetic relevance rests on Chebotarev equidistribution, which is asymptotic. So we check.

For each field, the splitting type of every unramified prime below a bound is computed by **distinct-degree factorization** over $\mathbb{F}_p$ — iteratively extracting $\gcd\big(x^{p^d} - x, f_{\text{rem}}\big)$, whose degree counts the irreducible factors of degree $d$. The residue dial is read from the maximal abelian subextension: a Legendre symbol for the $S_3$ and $S_4$ fields, $p \bmod 8$ for $x^4-2$, $p \bmod 5$ for $\Phi_5$.

{{algorithm:1}}

|---|---|---|---|---|
| $x^3+x+1$ | $S_3$ | $1.00000$ | $1.00000$ | $0.00000$ |
| $x^3-x+1$ | $S_3$ | $0.99998$ | $1.00000$ | $0.00002$ |
| $x^4-x-1$ | $S_4$ | $0.99985$ | $1.00000$ | $0.00015$ |
| $x^4-2$ | $D_4$ | $1.65930$ | $1.65564$ | $0.00366$ |
| $\Phi_5$ | $C_4$ | $1.49834$ | $1.50000$ | $0.00166$ |

<details>
<summary><b>Two estimator traps worth knowing about</b></summary>

**Sparse-modulus bias.** The naive plug-in estimator of mutual information is biased *upward* by roughly (number of free cells)$/(2n\ln 2)$ on a table with $n$ samples. For a several-hundred-cell semiprime table, a $3\times10^4$-sample estimate carries a bias near $0.10$ bits — quite enough to manufacture an apparent violation of a one-bit cap. Raising the sample count to $4\times10^5$ and checking against permutation nulls (independently reshuffling the dial) keeps the residual thickening at the $0.004$-bit level.

**The resolvent shortcut.** It is tempting to read a quartic splitting type off the factorization of the cubic resolvent. This is *invalid* for binomial and other special quartics: the axis pairing of $x^4-2$ is fixed by all of $D_4$, and for the $V_4$ field the resolvent splits over $\mathbb{Q}$. Types must be computed by genuine factor-degree extraction over $\mathbb{F}_p$, or equivalently by counting roots in $\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$.
</details>

## 9. Why it matters, and what is still open

**A budget for arithmetic side channels.** If a system exposes factorization shapes at primes tied to a secret, the law gives the adversary's exact per-observation yield about the residue class: $I = H(T) - H(T\mid\text{coset})$, bounded by $\log_2[G:G']$ and computable from a group table in time $O(\#G)$. Choosing a field with a small abelianization is a design decision with a quantified consequence; choosing a **perfect** Galois group makes the leak exactly zero.

**A quantitative frontier for reciprocity.** The abelian/non-abelian divide has always been described as a dichotomy. The law replaces it with a coordinate: every field is *partly* abelian, and the type channel measures that part in bits, interpolating from perfect groups (zero) to abelian groups (everything).

<details>
<summary><b>Open directions</b></summary>

* **Index-2 rigidity.** Every field in the table with abelianization $C_2$ attains its cap exactly. For an index-$2$ subgroup the coset readout is the sign of a permutation, and the sign is a function of the cycle type. Conjecture: if $[G:G']=2$ and the type readout comes from a faithful transitive action, the channel is complete, $I = 1$ exactly; more generally completeness holds precisely when the coset map factors through the cycle-type map, which for a transitive degree-$n$ action happens for every $G$ with $G' \supseteq G \cap A_n$.
* **Perfect-group flatness for $A_5$.** The general theorem is settled; the concrete prediction is that an $A_5$ quintic field has an identically zero channel at every level, following from the [simplicity of $A_5$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternating_group).
* **The $k$-almost-prime ladder.** Primes and semiprimes are $k = 1, 2$ of $I_k = I(\text{coset}(g_1\cdots g_k); \text{multiset of types})$. Conjecture: $I_k$ is non-increasing in $k$ and tends to $0$ unless the abelianization is an elementary abelian $2$-group, in which case it stabilises at a positive limit — one bit for $S_3$ and $S_4$.
</details>

---

## 10. The last word

The impossibility of solving the general quintic by radicals is the statement that $A_5$ is perfect — that it admits no abelian quotient. Two centuries later the same fact says something about information: a quintic field with that symmetry group is not merely resistant to congruence descriptions, it is **informationally silent**. No modulus, no progression, no quantity of data will ever reveal anything about how its polynomial falls apart.

Between that silence and the perfect transparency of quadratic reciprocity lies a continuum, and the continuum now has a coordinate: $\log_2$ of the index of the commutator subgroup, discounted by exactly how much the factorization shapes fail to see the cosets.

# The semiprime level: the pair law with the class-level type map

A semiprime `N = p q` presents the arithmetic reader with

* the **residue** of `N`, which by multiplicativity of the abelian characters is the
  *product* of the two Frobenius cosets, and
* the **unordered pair of splitting types** of `p` and `q` — unordered, because a
  factorisation-shape reader of `N` has no way of saying which factor carried which
  shape.

Modelling the two Frobenius elements as an independent uniform pair `(x, y) ∈ G × G`
(Chebotarev for the two factors), this file evaluates the semiprime channel

  `I₂ = I( coset(x·y) ; {T x, T y} )`

exactly, for all six fields, and proves the **which-factor wall**: replacing the
unordered pair `{T x, T y}` by the *ordered* pair `(T x, T y)` does not change the
channel by a single bit.  The reader learns nothing extra from being told which
factor carried which shape.

## The semiprime table (with `L3 = log₂ 3`, `L5 = log₂ 5`)

| field | `I₂` | numerically |
|---|---|---|
| `S₃` | `1` | `1.0000` |
| `S₄` | `1` | `1.0000` |
| `A₄` | `L3 - 10/9` | `0.47385` |
| `D₄` | `39/16 - (3/4)·L3 + (5/64)·L5` | `1.43018` |
| `V₄` | `19/8 - (21/16)·L3` | `0.29474` |
| `C₄` | `5/4` | `1.25000` |

The `S₃`/`S₄` rows are the **`C₂` cap at the semiprime level**: a five-type `S₄` field
still cannot push more than the one bit of its abelianization through a semiprime,
while `D₄`, whose abelianization is two-dimensional, goes above one bit.

/-- A numeric code for the splitting type, so that pairs of types can be ordered. -/
def typeCode {n : ℕ} (g : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℕ :=
  10 * (splitType g).1 + (splitType g).2

/-- The unordered pair of splitting types of the two prime factors. -/
def symType {n : ℕ} (p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) × Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℕ × ℕ :=
  (min (typeCode p.1) (typeCode p.2), max (typeCode p.1) (typeCode p.2))

/-- The ordered pair of splitting types: the readout of someone who is *also* told
which factor is which. -/
def ordType {n : ℕ} (p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) × Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℕ × ℕ :=
  (typeCode p.1, typeCode p.2)

/-- The residue readout of the semiprime: the coset of the product. -/
def prodCoset {n : ℕ} (c : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → ℕ)
    (p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) × Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℕ := c (p.1 * p.2)

# When is a splitting-type channel complete?

exactly the failure of that determination.

# Splitting types, Galois groups of small degree, and the arithmetic of `log₂`

This file supplies the concrete input for the type-channel law:

* the **splitting type readout** `splitType g` of a permutation of the roots, and the
  proof that it is a class function (`splitType_conj`) — this is what makes it the
  well-defined "factorisation shape of `p`" attached to the Frobenius *class*;
* the six Galois groups of the experiment, realised as explicit `Finset`s of
  permutations of the roots, with machine-checked certificates that each is a
  subgroup and that the stated `N` really is its derived subgroup
  (`IsDerivedFinset`), together with explicit numeric coset readouts;
* the small `log₂` arithmetic used to evaluate entropies in closed form.

## The type readout

For a squarefree `f` of degree `n ≤ 4` and an unramified `p`, the factorisation shape
of `f mod p` is the cycle type of Frobenius acting on the roots.  For `n ≤ 4` a cycle
type is determined by the pair

  `splitType g = (#fixed points of g, #points on 2-cycles of g)`,

namely `[1,1,1,1] ↦ (4,0)`, `[2,1,1] ↦ (2,2)`, `[2,2] ↦ (0,4)`, `[3,1] ↦ (1,0)`,
`[4] ↦ (0,0)` in degree 4, and `[1,1,1] ↦ (3,0)`, `[2,1] ↦ (1,2)`, `[3] ↦ (0,0)` in
degree 3.  Working with this pair keeps every count decidable.

## The fields

| field | `G` | `N = [G,G]` | `G/N` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x³ + x + 1` | `S₃` = `S3` | `A₃` = `A3` | `C₂` |
| `x⁴ - x - 1` | `S₄` = `S4` | `A₄` = `A4` | `C₂` |
| `x⁴ + 8x + 12` | `A₄` = `A4` | `V₄` = `V4` | `C₃` |
| `x⁴ - 2` | `D₄` = `D4` | `Z = {1, (02)(13)}` = `Z4c` | `C₂ × C₂` |
| `x⁴ - 2x² + 9` | `V₄` = `V4` | `1` | `V₄` |
| `Φ₅` | `C₄` = `C4` | `1` | `C₄` |

`D4` is realised as the stabiliser of the pairing `{{0,2},{1,3}}` of the roots
`α, iα, -α, -iα` of `x⁴ - 2`, which is exactly the Galois group of that field.
-/

namespace TypeChannel

open Finset Real Equiv

set_option maxRecDepth 4000000

/-! ### The splitting-type readout -/

/-- The splitting type of a permutation of `n` roots, recorded as the pair
(number of fixed points, number of points lying on 2-cycles).  For `n ≤ 4` this is a
faithful encoding of the cycle type, i.e. of the factorisation shape of the prime. -/
def splitType {n : ℕ} (g : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℕ × ℕ :=
  ((univ.filter (fun x : Fin n => g x = x)).card,
   (univ.filter (fun x : Fin n => g x ≠ x ∧ g (g x) = x)).card)

/-- **The type readout is a class function.**  Conjugate permutations have the same
splitting type; this is what makes "the splitting type of `p`" depend only on the
Frobenius *conjugacy class*, as Chebotarev's theorem requires. -/
theorem splitType_conj {n : ℕ} (g h : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
    splitType (h * g * h⁻¹) = splitType g := by
  unfold splitType
  have h1 : (univ.filter fun x : Fin n => (h * g * h⁻¹) x = x).card
      = (univ.filter fun x : Fin n => g x = x).card := by
    apply Finset.card_nbij' (fun x => h⁻¹ x) (fun x => h x) <;>
      intro x hx <;> simp_all [Equiv.Perm.mul_apply, Equiv.eq_symm_apply]
  have h2 : (univ.filter fun x : Fin n =>
        (h * g * h⁻¹) x ≠ x ∧ (h * g * h⁻¹) ((h * g * h⁻¹) x) = x).card
      = (univ.filter fun x : Fin n => g x ≠ x ∧ g (g x) = x).card := by
    apply Finset.card_nbij' (fun x => h⁻¹ x) (fun x => h x) <;>
      intro x hx <;> simp_all [Equiv.Perm.mul_apply, Equiv.eq_symm_apply]
  rw [h1, h2]

/-! ### The six Galois groups -/

/-- The parity readout, `0` for even and `1` for odd permutations: the coset readout of
the derived subgroup for `S₃` and `S₄`. -/
def signIdx {n : ℕ} (g : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℕ :=
  if Equiv.Perm.sign g = 1 then 0 else 1

/-- `S₃`, the Galois group of `x³ + x + 1` (and of `x³ - x + 1`). -/
def S3 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 3)) := univ

/-- `A₃`, the derived subgroup of `S₃`. -/
def A3 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 3)) := univ.filter (fun g => Equiv.Perm.sign g = 1)

/-- `S₄`, the Galois group of `x⁴ - x - 1`. -/
def S4 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) := univ

/-- `A₄`, the derived subgroup of `S₄`; also the Galois group of `x⁴ + 8x + 12`. -/
def A4 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) := univ.filter (fun g => Equiv.Perm.sign g = 1)

/-- `V₄`, the Klein four-group of double transpositions: the derived subgroup of `A₄`
and the Galois group of `x⁴ - 2x² + 9`. -/
def V4 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) :=
  univ.filter (fun g => splitType g = (4,0) ∨ splitType g = (0,4))

/-- `D₄`, the Galois group of `x⁴ - 2`: the stabiliser of the pairing
`{{0,2},{1,3}}` of the roots `α, iα, -α, -iα`. -/
def D4 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) :=
  univ.filter (fun g => ({g 0, g 2} : Finset (Fin 4)) = {0,2} ∨
    ({g 0, g 2} : Finset (Fin 4)) = {1,3})

/-- The centre of `D₄`, which is its derived subgroup. -/
def Z4c : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) :=
  univ.filter (fun g => g = 1 ∨ (g 0 = 2 ∧ g 1 = 3 ∧ g 2 = 0 ∧ g 3 = 1))

/-- `C₄`, the Galois group of `Φ₅`, acting regularly on the four roots. -/
def C4 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) :=
  univ.filter (fun g => g 1 = (g 0 + 1 : Fin 4) ∧ g 2 = (g 0 + 2 : Fin 4) ∧
    g 3 = (g 0 + 3 : Fin 4))

/-- The trivial subgroup. -/
def One4 : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) := {1}

/-- The `C₃`-coset readout for `A₄ / V₄`: which of the three pairings of the four
roots the pair `{g 0, g 1}` belongs to. -/
def pairIdx (g : Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) : ℕ :=
  if ({g 0, g 1} : Finset (Fin 4)) = {0,1} ∨ ({g 0, g 1} : Finset (Fin 4)) = {2,3} then 0
  else if ({g 0, g 1} : Finset (Fin 4)) = {0,2} ∨ ({g 0, g 1} : Finset (Fin 4)) = {1,3} then 1
  else 2

/-- The `C₂ × C₂`-coset readout for `D₄` modulo its centre: parity together with
whether the diagonal `{0,2}` is preserved. -/
def d4Idx (g : Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) : ℕ :=
  signIdx g + 2 * (if ({g 0, g 2} : Finset (Fin 4)) = {0,2} then 0 else 1)

/-- For a group acting regularly (`V₄`, `C₄`) the image of a single root already
separates the group elements, so it is the coset readout of the trivial subgroup. -/
def rootIdx (g : Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) : ℕ := (g 0 : ℕ)

/-! ### Subgroup and derived-subgroup certificates (machine checked) -/

lemma S3_isSubgroup : IsSubgroupFinset S3 := ⟨by decide, by decide, by decide⟩

lemma V4_isSubgroup : IsSubgroupFinset V4 := ⟨by decide, by decide, by decide⟩
lemma D4_isSubgroup : IsSubgroupFinset D4 := ⟨by decide, by decide, by decide⟩
lemma Z4c_isSubgroup : IsSubgroupFinset Z4c := ⟨by decide, by decide, by decide⟩
lemma C4_isSubgroup : IsSubgroupFinset C4 := ⟨by decide, by decide, by decide⟩
lemma One4_isSubgroup : IsSubgroupFinset One4 := ⟨by decide, by decide, by decide⟩

lemma S3_derived : IsDerivedFinset S3 A3 := ⟨by decide, by decide, by decide⟩

lemma S3_coset : IsCosetReadout S3 A3 signIdx := by
  unfold IsCosetReadout; decide
lemma S4_coset : IsCosetReadout S4 A4 signIdx := by
  unfold IsCosetReadout; decide

  unfold IsCosetReadout; decide

  unfold IsCosetReadout; decide

  unfold IsCosetReadout; decide

/-! ### `log₂` arithmetic -/

lemma logb2_two : logb 2 (2:ℝ) = 1 := Real.logb_self_eq_one (by norm_num)

lemma logb2_four : logb 2 (4:ℝ) = 2 := by
  rw [show (4:ℝ) = 2^(2:ℕ) by norm_num, Real.logb_pow]; simp

lemma neg_prob_logb (a n : ℕ) (ha : 0 < a) (hn : 0 < n) :
